blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Calculate total revenue and average revenue from price and sales figures, and explain how a change in sales moves revenue.

blocks.heading: Two formulas and their units
blocks.text: Total revenue = price x quantity sold, and average revenue = total revenue / quantity sold. Each answer carries its unit, N$. Marula Foods sells 800 jars of marula spread at N$25 a jar: total revenue = N$25 x 800 jars = N$20 000, and average revenue = N$20 000 / 800 jars = N$25, which is the price itself where each jar sells at the same figure.

blocks.heading: A price cut, worked through
blocks.text: To win more sales the firm cuts its price to N$20 a jar and sells 1 100 jars. Total revenue = N$20 x 1 100 jars = N$22 000, above the N$20 000 earned before, and average revenue = N$22 000 / 1 100 = N$20, the new price. The change in total revenue is N$22 000 - N$20 000 = N$2 000: the 300 extra jars added N$20 x 300 = N$6 000 against the N$5 x 800 = N$4 000 given up on the jars it had been selling at the higher price.

blocks.heading: How sales influence revenue
blocks.text: Where the price holds steady, more sales raise total revenue in step: ten more jars at N$25 add N$25 x 10 = N$250. Where the firm must cut its price to win sales, the outcome turns on whether the extra units add more income than the price cut gives up - the cut from N$25 to N$20 gave up N$5 on each of the 800 old jars, and the 300 new jars more than covered it. A fishing firm in Portugal reading its own sales figures applies the same test before it cuts a price.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: How strongly sales respond to a price change is the price elasticity of demand of topic 2.7; what the firm then does with its revenue is decided by the objectives of section 3.7.5, and the payments it makes are the costs of sections 3.7.1 and 3.7.2.
